source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: A training module under one hour improved Brier accuracy in every one of four tournament years versus randomly assigned no-training controls.
numbers: Brier improvement vs control: Y1 10% (probability) and 11% (scenario); Y2 12%; Y3 6%; Y4 7%.
quote: Although the training lasted less than one hour, it consistently improved accuracy (Brier scores) by 6 to 11%
limits: Volunteer forecasters (about 83% male, mean age 41, 67% some graduate study). Online, paid in gift certificates up to $250. Not a general population.
agent_relevance: The best-supported training effect in this series is a short, principle-based module. The size is modest (6 to 12%), so do not expect large gains from instructions alone.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Year 1 sample sizes and standardized Brier means for the three arms. Probability and scenario training did not differ.
numbers: Control n=152 M_std=+0.07 SD 0.28; probability-trained n=119 M=-0.05 SD 0.24; scenario-trained n=113 M=-0.06 SD 0.23; F(2,381)=12.1, p<.001; raw Brier 0.42 vs 0.38 vs 0.38.
limits: Only Year 1 had the two-module split; from Year 2 the modules were merged. Scores are standardized within question, so effects are relative to other forecasters, not absolute.
agent_relevance: Two framings of training gave the same gain, so the active ingredient is probably shared content (base rates, updating), not the framing.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Years 2 to 4 effect tests with N and statistics.
quote: Y4 means and n appear swapped in the running text
limits: The Year 4 running text lists trained n=131 and control n=102 with means in the opposite direction to Table 4, which lists no-training n=131 and training n=102. The paper is internally inconsistent here. The table direction matches the reported improvement. The effect shrinks from 12% to 6 to 7% in later years.
agent_relevance: Treat the early large numbers as an upper bound.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Of ten CHAMPS KNOW principles, self-reported use of comparison classes (reference classes) was the clearest link to accuracy. Post-mortem analysis and other-perspectives were linked to worse scores.
numbers: Mean standardized Brier of explanations: comparison classes n=580 M=0.17; all categorized trained explanations n=4,627 M=0.42; no category reported n=2,087 M=0.37; control explanations n=6,622 M=0.49. ANOVA (Table 6): comparison classes MS=39.34, F(1)=12.28, p<.001; only three principles were significant (C better; P and O worse).
quote: only three principles were significantly associated with mean standardized Brier scores
limits: Correlational: forecasters chose which principle box to tick, so selection effects are likely. Post-mortem is probably worse because it is applied after inaccurate forecasts (the authors say this). The principles were designed as a package, so effects are not separable.
agent_relevance: Of the guidance a scaffold could carry, the outside view (reference class) has the strongest link to accuracy. This supports an explicit reference-class step.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Probabilistic-reasoning principles (C, H, A, M, S) were associated with improvement. Political-reasoning principles (K, N, W) were not.
numbers: Table 7 ANOVA: probabilistic reasoning MS=38.51, F(1)=11.96, p<.001; political reasoning MS=0.24, F=0.08, p=.783 (after dropping P and O). 69% of trained forecasters' explanations were self-classified under a principle; 6,714 trained vs 6,622 control explanations; time spent 4.1 vs 3.7 hours per week, not different.
limits: Same correlational limits as b04. Domain-knowledge coaching showed no effect in this design.
agent_relevance: Generic reasoning training (base rates, updating, models) helped; domain-specific political coaching did not. This favors domain-free steps in the scaffold.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Training did not make people forecast more in total. Part of its effect was carried by targeted practice (more forecasts per question).
numbers: Mediation of training to accuracy by forecasts per question was supported in three of four years (Y2 indirect effect not significant; Y3 indirect effect -0.02, 95% CI -0.04 to -0.01). Total forecasts per person: Y1 86.76 control vs 84.29 probability-trained vs 73.15 scenario-trained.
limits: Mediation on observational data. Year 4 links were not significant (p=0.20 for one link).
agent_relevance: The gain may need repeated attempts on the same item (revisit and update), not a single pass. This fits a multi-pass scaffold with re-forecasting.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Cognitive ability predicted accuracy in all four years. Motivation measures did not. Training-by-ability interactions were mostly absent.
numbers: Cognitive ability (CRT, Berlin numeracy, Raven; composite) significant all four years; grit and active open-mindedness not significant; training had the highest explanatory power, then targeted practice, then ability; together they explained 10 to 20% of variance. In Y1 ability moderated training (ceiling for the most skilled); no significant interactions in later years.
limits: Numeracy and spatial reasoning alone did not predict. Self-selected, highly educated volunteers.
agent_relevance: Training helped people at different ability levels about equally after Year 1, so a fixed procedure is defensible; it is not only a crutch for weak reasoners.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: Prior tournament experience alone did not improve accuracy; training did.
numbers: Two-factor ANOVA on experience x training each year: training effect significant, main effect of veteran status not significant (Year 4 shown in Table 9).
limits: Veterans self-selected into returning. Question sets differ by year.
agent_relevance: Just doing the task is not enough; instruction or feedback is needed.

source: Chang, Chen, Mellers, Tetlock (2016) Developing expert political judgment: the impact of training and practice on judgmental accuracy in geopolitical forecasting tournaments
finding: The authors summarize why instruction-only debiasing often fails and what is stronger.
numbers: Cites mixed effects for confirmation-bias debiasing (Lilienfeld 2009; Weinstein and Klein 1995). Process-based override techniques (explaining reasoning patterns, asking the same question twice, reference-class teaching) beat merely naming biases (Ross, Lepper, Hubbard 1975; Fischhoff and Bar-Hillel 1984; Lovallo, Clarke, Camerer 2012).
quote: Informing people of biases is simply not enough
limits: Literature summary by the authors, not an independent test.
agent_relevance: Warning-label prompts ('beware overconfidence') are the weak form; procedures are the strong form.

source: Savage et al. (2021) A strategy to improve expert technology forecasts (PNAS; pilot study of briefings to reduce overconfidence)
finding: Two short videos on overconfidence widened 80% intervals, but respondents stayed overconfident. No accuracy feedback was given.
numbers: N=133 online respondents, three randomized groups (control, one briefing, two briefings of about 8 minutes in total). Two-briefing widened intervals on 8 of 10 questions (4 of 10 after Bonferroni); one-briefing 4 of 10 (1 of 10). Multilevel control vs two-briefing t=5.16, p<.001. All three groups' hit rates stayed below the 0.80 target (p<.001). Cited trivia example: only 48% of 80% intervals contained the answer.
quote: the treatment groups were less overconfident than the control group, but were still overconfident
limits: Pilot; informed volunteers, not experts; group sizes not fully reported; post hoc model; possible demand effects; accuracy of 2-year forecasts unresolved at the time; no effect size.
agent_relevance: Telling a model to widen its intervals will move width but may not fix calibration. Calibration needs outcome feedback or a post-hoc correction.

source: Doussau et al. (2023) The impact of feedback training on prediction of cancer clinical trial results (Clinical Trials)
finding: Failed training effect: a 3 to 4 minute feedback module did not improve expert predictions of cancer trial results.
numbers: 216 experts randomized, 148 analyzed; 25 phase 2/3 trials (13 positive), 1,217 forecasts. Brier control 0.22 (0.20 to 0.24) vs feedback 0.21 (0.20 to 0.23), p=0.51; AUC 0.70 vs 0.73, p=0.22; calibration index 0.10 vs 0.10, p=0.61. Uninformative 50% forecasts score 0.25.
quote: A short training module did not improve predictions for cancer trial results.
limits: Very short one-batch training with only 5 practice trials; the third (debiasing) arm was dropped after dropout; only 25 test trials; post hoc aggregate analysis; a module error affected 21 responses.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: minimal feedback in a hard, noisy domain gave a null effect. Dose and domain matter.

source: Doussau et al. (2023) feedback training (crowd result)
finding: Pooling the experts helped far more than training did.
numbers: Pooled crowd forecasts (post hoc, both arms combined per trial): Brier 0.17 (0.16 to 0.18), AUC 0.89 (0.85 to 0.92), calibration index 0.05 (0.04 to 0.06). Individual Brier 0.21 to 0.22. Leukemia forecasts (0.29) were no better than the 0.25 chance level (p=0.99).
limits: Post hoc; 25 trials only.
agent_relevance: Aggregation over many forecasts beat teaching a single forecaster. This fits G4 and G5 (code selects) and the aggregation subfield.

source: Superforecasting reality check: evidence from a small pool of experts and expedited identification (PLoS ONE 2020)
finding: A tournament run outside the US randomized forecasters to the standard GJP training (about 40 minutes) or that plus 20 minutes on decomposition and structured analogies. The extra module did not clearly change who became a top forecaster.
numbers: 314 registered, 195 fully engaged (Group A 86, Group B 109; the text gives 89 for A in one place). 14 questions (6 identification, 8 confirmation). Top 10%: 9 (B) vs 7 (A); top 25%: 24 vs 14; not significant. Only 2 superforecasters at the 2% cut. Median standardized score -0.437 (B) vs -0.252 (A).
limits: Small, unequal groups, one country, authors wrote the questions, no preregistered test of the training question. Dominance tests favored B, so the authors call it preliminary.
agent_relevance: Extra decomposition and analogy instruction showed a suggestive, not confirmed, gain. Do not assume more training minutes means more accuracy.

source: AI Impacts: Evidence on good forecasting practices from the Good Judgment Project
finding: Secondary source for the 'effect lasted a year' claim: a one-hour module in a randomized trial; effects persisted at least a year; training ranks below past performance, repeated predictions, deliberation time, teamwork, intelligence and expertise.
numbers: No numeric effect size on the page. Persistence is stated as a lower bound ('at least a year'). The page does not mention CHAMPS KNOW.
quote: its effects persisted for at least a year
limits: Secondary source. The Chang et al. text we opened reports within-year Brier gaps for each year and returning forecasters kept in their arm. We found no separate retention test in it.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on 'lasts a year' for design. An LLM has no persistence question; the module must be in the prompt every call.

source: Chang et al. (2016) cross-check of the persistence claim
finding: What the primary paper supports on durability: each year had its own randomly assigned trained and control groups, returning forecasters stayed in the same condition, and training effects were significant every year.
numbers: Training significant in Y1 to Y4 (6 to 12%); veteran experience alone not significant.
limits: Persistence for the same person over 12+ months is inferred from repeated yearly participation, not from a stated retention test.
agent_relevance: Mark 'effect lasted a year' as secondary-source and only partly supported.

source: Turtel, Franklin, Skotheim, Hewitt, Schoenegger (2025) Outcome-based Reinforcement Learning to Predict the Future (TMLR)
finding: Training (not prompting) an LLM on resolved binary questions with a Brier reward took a 14B model to o1 level on Brier and better calibration.
numbers: Train 10,000 Polymarket questions (+100,000 synthetic); test 1,265 questions. Soft-Brier: base DeepSeek-R1 14B 0.215 (ECE 0.089); ReMax ensemble-7 0.190 (ECE 0.062); Modified-GRPO 0.192 (ECE 0.054); o1 0.202 (ECE 0.093); Polymarket price 0.151 (ECE 0.043). ReMax vs base -0.025 (p<.001), vs o1 -0.011 (p<.05), vs market +0.039 (p<.001).
limits: The model did not beat the market price. One dataset of 1,265 questions. Hypothetical trading: $52 vs $39 for o1.
agent_relevance: The closest AI analogue of training. Brier-reward training helps, but our agent cannot be trained. It shows calibration gains come from outcome feedback, not instructions.

source: Turtel et al. (2025) outcome-based RL: reward design
finding: Training needed guardrails; training on outcomes after they were known caused overfitting.
numbers: Reward is negative Brier; collapse prevention over more than 100,000 sequential events; the best 10k-trained model (ReMax) had Brier 0.199 [0.187, 0.211] and ECE 0.067.
limits: Details are specific to RL fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: The reward is a proper scoring rule, the same logic as score feedback in the human tournaments.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025) Prompt Engineering Large Language Models' Forecasting Capabilities
finding: Instruction-style 'training' inside the prompt: of 38 prompts across 4 models, none significantly improved Brier and two hurt.
numbers: 100 ForecastBench binary questions; Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o, Llama 3.1 405B. Mixed-effects difference from control (negative is better): Frequency-Based Reasoning -0.014 (adj p=0.774); Base Rate First -0.011 (0.774); Chain of Thought -0.011 (0.774); Bayesian Reasoning +0.030 (adj p<0.001); Propose-Evaluate-Select +0.033 (adj p<0.001).
limits: Preregistered but only 100 questions resolving end of 2024.
agent_relevance: Prompting alone did not reproduce the human training effect. Do not add 'think like a superforecaster' or Bayesian recipes to the schema without a test (G7).

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025) Prompt Engineering: Study 2
finding: Compound prompts and externally sourced forecasting prompts were no better; the superforecaster-authored odds-ratio prompt made forecasts worse.
numbers: Study 2 added o1 (mean Brier 0.216) and o1-mini (0.217). Superforecaster-authored Conditional Odds-Ratio prompt +0.023 vs control (z=4.165, adj p=0.01).
limits: Same 100 questions; small effect sizes.
agent_relevance: A human-expert recipe can backfire for LLMs. Only measured steps get in.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2025) Prompt Engineering: forecast spread
finding: Prompts changed how far forecasts moved from 0.5 without improving accuracy.
numbers: Bayesian Reasoning, Propose-Evaluate-Select and Chain of Thought made forecasts more decisive (17.2 to 19.9 percentage points from midpoint on average); Control, Re-Reading and Anti-Biasing (Anchoring) stayed 11.9 to 13.4 points from the midpoint.
limits: Description of the forecast distribution only.
agent_relevance: Prompts that push extremity are the ones that hurt; keeping forecasts nearer the base rate is safer.

source: Chandak, Goel, Prabhu, Hardt, Geiping (2025) Scaling Open-Ended Reasoning to Predict the Future (OpenForesight)
finding: RL on auto-generated forecasting questions improved accuracy, Brier and consistency of an 8B model, and the calibration gain carried over to other benchmarks.
numbers: OpenForesight training set 52K questions (about 248K source articles; over 90% of generated questions removed by filters; validity check 95% by Qwen3-32B given the article). Retrieval adds 9 to 18% accuracy across models; gains plateau after 5 chunks. Test: held-out questions May to August 2025.
limits: Open-ended questions with the authors' own scoring; final headline numbers are in figures we did not capture as text.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of dated news gave a large lift without training; the training gain is separate and available only to those who can fine-tune.

source: Chandak et al. (2025) OpenForesight reward ablation
finding: Rewarding accuracy alone ruins calibration; Brier alone stalls exploration; the sum is best.
numbers: Accuracy-only reward led to negative Brier-style scores, worse than a constant 0 baseline. The Brier-only model answered 'Unknown' at near-zero confidence in about 40% of samples vs about 4% for accuracy + Brier.
limits: Validation set; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct was used for the scaling runs.
agent_relevance: If we ever score the agent's own forecasts, include accuracy and calibration together; calibration alone invites abstention (G6).

source: Damani et al. (2025) Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty (RLCR)
finding: Standard right-or-wrong RL worsens calibration; adding a Brier term on stated confidence fixes it without losing accuracy.
numbers: Reported expected calibration error fell from 0.37 to 0.03 on HotpotQA and from 0.26 to 0.10 on a math collection (contribution list). Trained on 20,000 HotpotQA examples. Out of domain (TriviaQA, SimpleQA, MATH500, GSM8K, CommonsenseQA, GPQA) RLVR worsened calibration and RLCR improved it.
limits: Factual QA and math, not forecasting; the 'from X to Y' arrow was lost in text extraction, direction inferred from context.
agent_relevance: A scoring-rule signal during learning is what produces calibration, not instruction text.

source: Schoenegger, Park, Karger, Trott, Tetlock (2024) AI-Augmented Predictions: LLM Assistants Improve Human Forecasting Accuracy (abstract read)
finding: Humans advised by a frontier LLM forecast better, even when the LLM was deliberately overconfident and ignored base rates.
numbers: N=991, six questions. Either frontier assistant raised accuracy 24 to 28% vs control; excluding one outlier item, the superforecasting assistant +41% and the noisy assistant +29%.
limits: Abstract only; one outlier item drove results; hypotheses on skill, diversity and difficulty were not consistently supported.
agent_relevance: Advice from a strong model acts like on-demand training for humans. A second-pass consultation inside our agent should be tested.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration (abstract read)
finding: Verbalized confidence from RLHF chat models is better calibrated than their token probabilities.
numbers: Often a relative 50% reduction in expected calibration error; ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude on TriviaQA, SciQ, TruthfulQA.
limits: Abstract only; QA tasks, not forecasting.
agent_relevance: A cheap prompt-level step (state a confidence in words) is worth a test; it is the one instruction-type calibration gain found here.

source: Lin, Hilton, Evans (2022) Teaching Models to Express Uncertainty in Words (abstract read)
finding: GPT-3 fine-tuned on verbalized probabilities stays calibrated under distribution shift (CalibratedMath).
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; fine-tuning, arithmetic tasks.
agent_relevance: Training verbalized confidence generalizes; prompting alone was not shown here.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know (abstract read)
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple choice when formatted properly; P(True) improves when the model sees many of its own samples; trained P(IK) generalizes only partly.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Calibration on new tasks is weaker.
agent_relevance: Supports sample-then-judge, but G4 reminds us that samples from one model are not independent.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Forecasting Future World Events with Neural Networks (Autocast, abstract read)
finding: Early LLMs were far below a human expert baseline on forecasting questions; accuracy rose with model size and with access to relevant news.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract (thousands of questions).
limits: Abstract only; old models.
agent_relevance: Retrieval of news, not instruction, was the lever.

source: Pratt, Blumberg, Carolino, Morris (2024) Can Language Models Use Forecasting Strategies? (abstract read)
finding: LLM forecasters remained inaccurate and tended to predict that most events would not happen.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Beware a systematic 'No' bias; correct with base rates measured from data.
